turns.user: Export robot_arm.ocad.d as a URDF into urdf/ so I can simulate it in MuJoCo.

steps.assistant:
I exported the arm to `urdf/`. I haven't loaded it in MuJoCo yet, so it's untested in the simulator.

**What was written:**
- `urdf/robot_arm.urdf`
- One STL mesh per part next to it: `robot_arm_assembly_001_base.stl`, `…_upper_arm.stl`, `…_forearm.stl` and `…_gripper.stl` (4,296 triangles in total).

**How the robot is set up:**
- **Links:** `base` (the fixed part of the assembly, 382 g), then `upper_arm` (186 g), `forearm` (107 g) and `gripper` (60 g).
- **Joints:** `shoulder`, `elbow` and `wrist`. All three rotate freely around the Z axis.
- **Starting pose:** each joint's zero angle is the pose the assembly is in now, so the elbow starts rotated −45° (−0.785 rad).

**Before you simulate:**
- **Masses come from an assumed material.** The exporter calculated them from the geometry using aluminium's density (2700 kg/m³). If the parts are made of something else, the masses and inertias will be off.
- **The joints have no limits, damping or motors.** MuJoCo won't drive anything on its own; you need to add actuators to the MJCF model after import. If the joints should have a limited range, that has to be added to the design rather than typed into the URDF.
- **Loading:** run `python -m mujoco.viewer --mjcf urdf/robot_arm.urdf`, or call `mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path("urdf/robot_arm.urdf")`. The mesh paths are relative, so keep the STLs in the same folder as the URDF.

The URDF is generated from the design, so if the design changes, re-export it instead of editing the file by hand.
